transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. What brings you to see me today?

Well, Doctor, I... I came in because things have been getting really out of hand at my apartment building. It's not just a feeling, it's something I've been watching happen day after day. See, I know the people there—my neighbors, the maintenance guys, probably even the people across the hall—they're all watching me. They track my comings and goings. Every time I leave to go to the store, or just step out to get some air, I can feel eyes on me, and I know they're keeping a log or something. And it doesn't stop there. They’ve been slipping these notes about me to the front office. I've seen the papers getting passed around, or stuck to doors. Now, my sister and the building manager, everybody keeps telling me, "Oh, it's just regular notices on the doors, it's just reminders about the trash or the water being shut off." But they don't see what I see. They don't understand that these aren't just regular flyers. It's a whole coordinated thing, and it's exhausting, you know? Just trying to live your life when everyone is keeping tabs on you and reporting back to the office. I just... I can't get anyone to listen to me about what's really going on with these notes.
That sounds very stressful to deal with. Have you ever heard voices talking or whispering when no one was physically around you?

No, no, I've never had anything like that. I mean, I don't hear voices or whispers or anything spooky like that when I'm alone in my apartment. It's not like that at all. It's the real people, you see? The actual people in the building. I can hear them talking out in the hall, or down in the lobby, and I know they're talking about me. I can hear the murmur of their voices through the door sometimes, just low enough that I can't make out every single word, but I know the tone. I know what they're doing. But it's not like I'm sitting in my living room and hearing voices coming out of the walls or thin air. It's the neighbors, the maintenance man, the people who are actually there, physically there, watching and whispering to each other when they think I'm not paying attention. But I am paying attention. I have to, right? With everything going on, I have to keep my ears open. But no, no invisible voices. Just the real ones, plotting.
About how long has this been going on with your neighbors?

Well, let me think on that. It doesn't just start all at once, you know, it sort of creeps up on you. But if I really put a pin in it, to when I first knew for sure what they were doing... it’s been about a year and a month. Yeah, a year and a month. I know that because it was right around the time they sent out those new parking rules last year. I went down to the office to ask about it, and the lady behind the desk gave me this look. Just a real knowing look, like she had a file on me right there under the counter. 

And ever since then, for a whole year and a month, it’s been non-stop. Every time I walk down the hall, every time I take my trash out. You try living like that for over a year, doctor. Thirteen whole months of watching them watch me. It wears a man down, it really does. I mean, I don't work anymore, so I'm home a lot, which means I see it all happen. I see the maintenance guy sweeping the exact same spot in the lobby for twenty minutes just waiting to see when I check my mail. A year and a month of this... it's just too much for one person to handle, but they don't care. They just keep at it, day in and day out, logging everything I do, passing those notes around. Thirteen months of it.
Aside from the stress of this situation, have you been experiencing persistent feelings of sadness, depression, or a loss of interest in things you used to enjoy?

Well... yeah. I mean, it's hard to separate it all out, isn't it? The stress and the sadness, they kind of bleed into each other. But yes, the sadness... it's heavy. It's really heavy. It's not just feeling a little down because of the neighbors, it's... it's deeper than that. 

Most mornings, I wake up with this heavy, hollow feeling in my chest. It's like... like the day already went bad before I even get my feet on the floor. I open my eyes, and there's just this immediate weight pressing down on me, telling me there's no point in getting up. And I used to like doing things, you know? I used to like tinkering with old radios, fixing them up. I had a whole workbench set up in the corner of my living room. I'd spend hours just fiddling with the dials and the wires, getting the static just right. But now... I look at that workbench and I feel absolutely nothing. The dust is just piling up on it. I haven't touched a radio in months. I just sit in my chair, staring at the wall, feeling that hollow ache. It's like all the color has been drained out of everything. 

And it's not just the radios, it's everything. I don't even care about watching my shows anymore. I used to watch the history channel every night, but now the TV just stays off. It's too much effort to even pick up the remote. I just sit there, feeling so empty, so incredibly sad, and it just doesn't lift. It stays with me all day, no matter what I do. It's like carrying a sack of wet sand around with me everywhere I go in that apartment. And when you combine that with knowing everyone is watching you... it's just... it's a lot, doctor. It really is.

It's been... gosh, it's been about a year and two months now. Yes, a year and two months. Because I remember it was late summer, right before the leaves started turning, when I first felt that sack of wet sand just drop onto my chest and refuse to budge. I'd wake up and just... stare. Just stare at the ceiling for an hour before I could even swing my legs over the side of the bed. And then a month later, that's when the parking rules came out, and that lady at the desk gave me that look, and all the whispering started. 

But the sadness, that deep, draining feeling where I just pulled away from everything I used to care about... that was already there. It had already set in. Fourteen months of waking up feeling like the day is ruined before it begins, fourteen months of not caring if a tube blew in one of my favorite radios, fourteen months of just... existing in this gray fog. It feels like an eternity, doctor, it really does. You try carrying that weight for over a year, and then on top of it, everyone starts plotting against you just a month later. It’s a year and two months of the heavy feeling, and it hasn't let up for a single day. Not one single day.

I never had days where I felt like I could take on the world or run a marathon without sleeping. 

Sleep was always something I needed, you know? I know some folks get like that, where they get all wound up and talk a mile a minute and stay up for three days straight painting their house or whatever it is they do. But me? Never. If anything, I've always been on the slower side, just taking my time with things. Especially with the radios, you have to be patient. You can't be rushing around with all that nervous energy or you'll snap a delicate wire or solder the wrong connection. You have to have a steady hand and a quiet mind for that. 

So, no, I haven't ever had a time where I felt like I was, you know, buzzing or didn't need to rest. It's always just been either regular life, just getting by day to day, or... or this. This awful, heavy wet sand feeling I was telling you about. There's never been an opposite to that for me, never a time where I felt high as a kite or like my thoughts were racing a hundred miles an hour. I just don't have that kind of motor in me, never have. I've always just been even-keeled, right up until the sadness started dragging me down into the floorboards.

Guilty? I... well, I don't know about guilty, exactly. It's more like... like I just don't matter. Like I'm just taking up space in that apartment, you know? It's not that I think I committed a crime or did something terrible to someone in the past. I haven't hurt anybody. I've always tried to keep to myself, just me and my radios. 

But worthlessness... yeah, that's a word for it. That heavy feeling I was telling you about, the wet sand? It's not just a physical weight, it's a mental one, too. I sit in that chair all day, staring at the wall, and I just think, "What is the point of me? What am I even doing here?" I'm 59 years old, I don't work anymore, I didn't even finish high school... I mean, I left in the 11th grade to help my uncle with his shop, and I always meant to go back and get my diploma, but life just gets away from you, doesn't it? The years just slip by while you're busy trying to make ends meet. And now, here I am. 

I look at that dusty workbench, and I think about how I used to be able to fix things. I used to be able to take a broken, silent box and make it sing again. I had a purpose, even if it was just a small one. But now... I can't even fix myself. I can't even get out of a chair to turn on the TV. I just feel so completely useless. Like if I just disappeared tomorrow, nothing would change. The world would just keep spinning, the neighbors would keep whispering, and nobody would even notice I was gone. It's a terrible thing to feel, doctor. To sit there hour after hour, day after day, and just feel like you are absolutely nothing. Like you're just a ghost haunting your own living room. So, guilty? No, not guilty. Just... empty. Just completely, utterly worthless.

Well, as far as... hurting myself, like actually doing something to end it all? No. No, I don't have a plan for anything like that. I don't sit there figuring out ways to do it, or gathering things up, or looking out the window thinking about jumping. I don't have the energy for that, to be honest. And I don't want to cause a mess for anyone else to clean up. I've always tried to be neat, you know? Keep my things organized, my tools in their place. 

But... do I think about death? Yes. Yes, I do. A lot, actually. It's not like I'm actively trying to make it happen, but I catch myself sitting there in the quiet, especially when the gray fog is really thick and the neighbors are being loud, and I just think... it would be all right. It really would be perfectly fine if I went to sleep tonight and just didn't wake up tomorrow. 

It wouldn't be a tragedy, doctor. It would just be... quiet. Finally quiet. No more heavy wet sand on my chest, no more feeling like I'm taking up space, no more messing things up or just existing for no reason. Sometimes I lie in bed and I just pray, I really do, I just say, "Please, just let me slip away." Just a quiet slip into nothingness where I don't have to carry this anymore. Where I don't have to worry about the people in the building or the radios I can't fix or the fact that I'm 59 and I have absolutely nothing to show for it. So, no, I'm not going to do anything to myself, I'm not going to hurt myself. But if the end just came on its own, if it just swept in while I was sleeping... I wouldn't fight it. I think I'd welcome it, honestly. It just seems like it would be a relief to just... stop.

My appetite? Well... it's just like everything else, doctor. It's just sort of faded away into the gray. I used to enjoy a good meal, you know? Back when I was working with my uncle at the shop, we’d close up and go down to the diner on the corner and get a hot roast beef sandwich, maybe some mashed potatoes with gravy. Good, solid food that stuck to your ribs and made you feel alive. 

But now? Now I don't even think about food. I just sit in my chair, like I told you, with that heavy wet sand feeling pressing me down into the cushions, and the hours just tick by. I completely forget to eat. The whole morning goes, the afternoon goes, and suddenly it's late in the day, maybe five or six o'clock, and the sun is starting to go down and cast those long shadows across the living room floor, and it dawns on me that I haven't had a single bite of anything. 

And even then, when I finally realize my stomach is empty, I just don't have the drive to get up and actually make anything. The thought of standing at the stove, getting out a pan, opening up cans... it just feels like climbing a mountain. It's too much. So all I can really manage is just... a cup of coffee and maybe a piece of toast. That's it. That's all I can bring myself to make. 

And you can imagine what living on coffee and a single piece of toast does to a man. I've been losing weight, I know I have. I don't have a scale in the bathroom to check the exact numbers, but I can feel it. My pants, the same ones I've worn for years, they've just been hanging loose on me lately. I have to pull my belt a notch or two tighter just to keep them up when I do manage to shuffle into the kitchen. It's like I'm just shrinking away. Shrinking right out of my clothes, just fading away to nothing while the days blur together. So, no, the appetite just isn't there anymore.
Before this deep sadness began fourteen months ago, had you ever felt that people were watching you or plotting against you?

Well, the neighbors... that’s a whole different story, doctor. It’s not just tied up with this heavy, wet sand feeling that’s been crushing me for the last fourteen months. Even before I got completely stuck in my chair, long before the gray fog got this thick, I knew what they were doing out there. Living in an apartment building like mine, you get to know the sounds of the place, and you know when things aren't right. 

Actually, I remember there was this one spell, just a few weeks, where the fog actually lifted a little bit. I was actually eating a bit better—maybe fixing a real sandwich instead of just forcing down dry toast—and I wasn't waking up feeling quite so completely hopeless every single morning. I thought to myself, "Maybe I'm getting my energy back. Maybe I can finally get back to my workbench and look at those radios." 

But even then... even when the sadness backed off for a minute and I had a little bit of strength, I still knew they were out there. I still believed the neighbors were watching my door and reporting on me. I'd hear the floorboards creak out in the hall, or I'd see a shadow pass under the gap at the bottom of the doorframe, and I just knew they were keeping a log of everything I did. When my lights went on, when I ran the water, if I even walked near the peephole... they were keeping track. I don't know exactly who they report to—the landlord, maybe someone else, I really couldn't tell you—but it never stopped. It makes you feel like a prisoner in your own home, it really does. You try to just mind your own business, but you can feel their eyes on you right through the wood. So, yes, long before the deep sadness took over, and even during the times I felt a little bit of relief from the heavy feeling, the watching... the watching never stopped.

Guilty? I... well, I don't know about guilty, exactly. It's more like... like I just don't matter. Like I'm just taking up space in that apartment, you know? It's not that I think I committed a crime or did something terrible to someone in the past. I haven't hurt anybody. I've always tried to keep to myself, just me and my radios. 

But worthlessness... yeah, that's a word for it. That heavy feeling I was telling you about, the wet sand? It's not just a physical weight, it's a mental one, too. I sit in that chair all day, staring at the wall, and I just think, "What is the point of me? What am I even doing here?" I'm 59 years old, I don't work anymore, I didn't even finish high school... I mean, I left in the 11th grade to help my uncle with his shop, and I always meant to go back and get my diploma, but life just gets away from you, doesn't it? The years just slip by while you're busy trying to make ends meet. And now, here I am. 

I look at that dusty workbench, and I think about how I used to be able to fix things. I used to be able to take a broken, silent box and make it sing again. I had a purpose, even if it was just a small one. But now... I can't even fix myself. I can't even get out of a chair to turn on the TV. I just feel so completely useless. Like if I just disappeared tomorrow, nothing would change. The world would just keep spinning, the neighbors would keep whispering, and nobody would even notice I was gone. It's a terrible thing to feel, doctor. To sit there hour after hour, day after day, and just feel like you are absolutely nothing. Like you're just a ghost haunting your own living room. So, guilty? No, not guilty. Just... empty. Just completely, utterly worthless.

patient.answer:
Well, as far as... hurting myself, like actually doing something to end it all? No. No, I don't have a plan for anything like that. I don't sit there figuring out ways to do it, or gathering things up, or looking out the window thinking about jumping. I don't have the energy for that, to be honest. And I don't want to cause a mess for anyone else to clean up. I've always tried to be neat, you know? Keep my things organized, my tools in their place. 

But... do I think about death? Yes. Yes, I do. A lot, actually. It's not like I'm actively trying to make it happen, but I catch myself sitting there in the quiet, especially when the gray fog is really thick and the neighbors are being loud, and I just think... it would be all right. It really would be perfectly fine if I went to sleep tonight and just didn't wake up tomorrow. 

It wouldn't be a tragedy, doctor. It would just be... quiet. Finally quiet. No more heavy wet sand on my chest, no more feeling like I'm taking up space, no more messing things up or just existing for no reason. Sometimes I lie in bed and I just pray, I really do, I just say, "Please, just let me slip away." Just a quiet slip into nothingness where I don't have to carry this anymore. Where I don't have to worry about the people in the building or the radios I can't fix or the fact that I'm 59 and I have absolutely nothing to show for it. So, no, I'm not going to do anything to myself, I'm not going to hurt myself. But if the end just came on its own, if it just swept in while I was sleeping... I wouldn't fight it. I think I'd welcome it, honestly. It just seems like it would be a relief to just... stop.

patient.answer:
My appetite? Well... it's just like everything else, doctor. It's just sort of faded away into the gray. I used to enjoy a good meal, you know? Back when I was working with my uncle at the shop, we’d close up and go down to the diner on the corner and get a hot roast beef sandwich, maybe some mashed potatoes with gravy. Good, solid food that stuck to your ribs and made you feel alive. 

But now? Now I don't even think about food. I just sit in my chair, like I told you, with that heavy wet sand feeling pressing me down into the cushions, and the hours just tick by. I completely forget to eat. The whole morning goes, the afternoon goes, and suddenly it's late in the day, maybe five or six o'clock, and the sun is starting to go down and cast those long shadows across the living room floor, and it dawns on me that I haven't had a single bite of anything. 

And even then, when I finally realize my stomach is empty, I just don't have the drive to get up and actually make anything. The thought of standing at the stove, getting out a pan, opening up cans... it just feels like climbing a mountain. It's too much. So all I can really manage is just... a cup of coffee and maybe a piece of toast. That's it. That's all I can bring myself to make. 

And you can imagine what living on coffee and a single piece of toast does to a man. I've been losing weight, I know I have. I don't have a scale in the bathroom to check the exact numbers, but I can feel it. My pants, the same ones I've worn for years, they've just been hanging loose on me lately. I have to pull my belt a notch or two tighter just to keep them up when I do manage to shuffle into the kitchen. It's like I'm just shrinking away. Shrinking right out of my clothes, just fading away to nothing while the days blur together. So, no, the appetite just isn't there anymore.

doctor.question: Before this deep sadness began fourteen months ago, had you ever felt that people were watching you or plotting against you?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 3
target_item.manifestation: There was a spell of several weeks when I was eating a bit better and not waking up so hopeless, but I still believed the neighbors were watching my door and reporting on me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the delusions occurred before or independently of the depressive episode, which assesses whether psychotic symptoms were present in the absence of a major mood episode (Criterion B).

patient.answer:
Well, the neighbors... that’s a whole different story, doctor. It’s not just tied up with this heavy, wet sand feeling that’s been crushing me for the last fourteen months. Even before I got completely stuck in my chair, long before the gray fog got this thick, I knew what they were doing out there. Living in an apartment building like mine, you get to know the sounds of the place, and you know when things aren't right. 

Actually, I remember there was this one spell, just a few weeks, where the fog actually lifted a little bit. I was actually eating a bit better—maybe fixing a real sandwich instead of just forcing down dry toast—and I wasn't waking up feeling quite so completely hopeless every single morning. I thought to myself, "Maybe I'm getting my energy back. Maybe I can finally get back to my workbench and look at those radios." 

But even then... even when the sadness backed off for a minute and I had a little bit of strength, I still knew they were out there. I still believed the neighbors were watching my door and reporting on me. I'd hear the floorboards creak out in the hall, or I'd see a shadow pass under the gap at the bottom of the doorframe, and I just knew they were keeping a log of everything I did. When my lights went on, when I ran the water, if I even walked near the peephole... they were keeping track. I don't know exactly who they report to—the landlord, maybe someone else, I really couldn't tell you—but it never stopped. It makes you feel like a prisoner in your own home, it really does. You try to just mind your own business, but you can feel their eyes on you right through the wood. So, yes, long before the deep sadness took over, and even during the times I felt a little bit of relief from the heavy feeling, the watching... the watching never stopped.
